summary: Discusses lessons learned from InterNIC Directory and Database Services' development and operation of WWWSeeker, an application that finds a web site from the name and location of an organization, using DNS as a source. It is an experience report.

plainLanguage.summary: A team built a finder that guesses a company's web address from its name and town. This document shares what they learned from trying it.

questions: finding a website from an organization name
subtitle: How to build a directory of companies and their web sites from domain registries

tldr.problem: People want to find a company's website by knowing only the company name and location, but guessing domain names is hard: there are many top-level domains and companies do not always use obvious names.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC describes how InterNIC's WWWSeeker application built a searchable directory by collecting domain information from registries using WHOIS and other protocols, then maintaining it through automated updates.
tldr.outcome: The project demonstrated that a practical directory can be built from publicly available registry data, though maintaining accuracy and keeping up with domain growth requires careful engineering.

today: RFC 2517 is an Informational RFC documenting the InterNIC WWWSeeker project experience, which concluded in March 1998. While the specific system is no longer maintained, the lessons about directory building from registry data remain relevant for modern directory and search services.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Before search engines became common, there was no easy way to find a website if you did not already know its address. If you wanted to find the web site of a company, you had to guess its domain name: maybe www.companyname.com, or www.companyname.net, or perhaps the country code domain for the company's location.

The problem grew worse as domain names multiplied. With many countries using two-letter domain codes (.uk, .ca, .de) alongside generic top-level domains (.com, .net, .org, .edu), guessing became nearly impossible. The InterNIC Directory and Database Services project created WWWSeeker, an application that found web sites given the organization name and location, powered by a back-end database built from domain registry data.

This RFC documents the experience and lessons learned from building and maintaining that directory from July 1996 until the project shut down in March 1998.
sections.plainLanguage: Imagine trying to find a store's phone number when all you know is the store name and city. You do not have a phone book, so you have to guess. A team built a tool that makes this easier for websites.

sections.title: Building the Directory
sections.content:
Creating a directory required solving two distinct problems: discovering which domain names exist (building the skeleton) and gathering information about the organizations that own them (adding the meat).

The initial instinct to use DNS tree walks proved impractical. Tree walks scan all DNS zones to discover domains, but the Internet community discourages them because the namespace changes so frequently (150,000 to 200,000 new domains per month in 1998) that new tree walks would be needed monthly or more often. Instead, the team discovered that bulk retrieval from domain registries using FTP, HTTP or Gopher was far more efficient. Information is often available from the registries directly, and this method gathered both domain names and organization information at the same time.

For organization details, the team used the WHOIS protocol to query registries about domain owners. At project end, the database contained about 2.9 million records gathered this way, with an additional 360,000 records from other sources. However, WHOIS data contains many typographical errors and is often incomplete, covering only second-level domains (like ne.us) rather than subdomains. The team found that supporting multiple retrieval methods was necessary because some registries used WHOIS, others offered HTTP or FTP access, and some had no public data at all.
sections.plainLanguage: Finding every domain one at a time is too slow. The team found that asking domain registries directly (like asking a phone company for a list of customers) worked better. They had to use several different ways to ask different registries.

sections.title: Maintaining the Database
sections.content:
Keeping the directory current was a major challenge. A complete rebuild from all available WHOIS data would take 134 to 168 days on a Sun SPARCstation 20, not counting other processing like building search indexes (which alone took 24 hours). Given that 150,000 to 200,000 new domains were being registered each month, a fresh rebuild every month was infeasible.

The solution was incremental updates: the team saved the list of known domains (a checkpoint) and rebuilt the database incrementally during one weekend each month. This approach, supported by only 1 to 4 machines, completed the update in a couple of days. During other weeks, the team refreshed existing records when underlying information changed, trading some staleness for manageable resource requirements.

For searching, the team used a simple but effective approach: a flat ASCII file containing all records, searched via Perl scripts that built an inverted index tree. Despite its simplicity, this system handled over 200,000 database queries per month. The team noted that migrating to a proper database management system was not yet necessary, though it would likely improve scalability.
sections.plainLanguage: The database was too big to rebuild from scratch every month. Instead, they saved their progress and added just the new domains each month. They used simple tools to search the database, and it worked for 200,000 searches per month.

sections.title: Interoperability and Security
sections.content:
The data in such a directory is already public through WHOIS and DNS, so the directory itself does not create new security holes. However, it does make searching easier, and easier searching could make it easier for attackers to enumerate systems or companies to target. More concerning, the underlying data quality issues are amplified: typographical errors and incomplete information from WHOIS become widespread through a larger directory.

The protocols used (WHOIS, DNS, FTP, HTTP) have no built-in security features. If a source machine is spoofed while gathering data, the directory could be populated with incorrect information, which then spreads to everyone using it. The team recommended treating registry data as public, protecting the directory's query service against abuse, and being cautious about relying on data quality that is already questionable.
sections.plainLanguage: The information comes from public records, so the directory does not reveal secrets. But bad information gets bigger when shared more widely, so the team had to be careful about accuracy.

sections.title: Lessons for Future Implementors
sections.content:
The key lessons from WWWSeeker are practical: use bulk retrieval from registries rather than DNS tree walks; support multiple data sources and protocols because registries vary widely; use incremental updates to keep a large database current without overwhelming your infrastructure; keep new data separate and validate it before merging; and recognize that data quality is a perennial problem requiring careful handling.

The project demonstrated that a directory serving 200,000+ monthly queries was achievable with 1970s-style file and index technology. The team also documented that while a purely monolithic (non-distributed) database served their needs, migration to database technology would have improved both performance and scalability. This experience report provides concrete evidence for what does and does not work when building Internet directories from registry data.
sections.plainLanguage: Ask registries directly instead of trying to figure it out yourself. Be ready to handle many different ways they share data. Update regularly, not all at once. Accept that the data will not be perfect.
